direct_claims: This dataset reports the share of surveyed young people aged 16 to 25 who answered "yes" to six statements about climate change in 2021 across ten named countries plus an all-countries aggregate.
The source is Our World in Data, based on accessibility metadata linking to the grapher page.
The expert domain story states that 1,000 young people were surveyed in each country.
The six statements span existential fear, family security, economic opportunity, childbearing hesitation, fear about the future, and belief that people have failed to care for the planet.

In this chart, each number is a percentage of surveyed young people in a country who said "yes" to a specific climate-related statement, not a measure of emissions, temperature change, or policy strength.
Because each country surveyed 1,000 young people, each percentage corresponds roughly to the share within that sample rather than the entire national youth population.
The all-countries row is presented as an aggregate in the supplied data, but the metadata does not explain its weighting method.
Because no stakeholder context is provided, specific decision users cannot be identified from the metadata alone.
derived_claims: Across the listed countries, the highest overall agreement is with "People have failed to take care of the planet" at 83% in the all-countries row, while the lowest is "Hesitant to have children" at 39%. — derived by comparing the six values in the All countries row.

The country values vary substantially by statement; for example, "Future is frightening" ranges from 56% in Finland to 92% in the Philippines. — derived by reading minimum and maximum across country rows for that statement.

Brazil, India, and the Philippines tend to have some of the highest percentages across multiple statements, while Finland and the United States often appear toward the lower end. — derived by comparing relative levels across countries and statements.

The strongest all-countries responses are emotional and moral judgments: 75% say the future is frightening and 83% say people have failed to take care of the planet. — derived by reading the All countries values for those two statements.

Material and life-course concerns are also prominent: 55% say they will have less opportunity than their parents and 52% say family security is threatened. — derived by reading the All countries values for those statements.

Hesitation to have children is lower than the other concerns in every listed row, ranging from 23% in Nigeria to 48% in Brazil. — derived by comparing all country values in the hesitant-to-have-children column.

This suggests that reproductive hesitation is a more selective response than general fear or blame, at least within these survey items. — derived by comparing the consistently lower childbearing-hesitation percentages against the other statement percentages across rows.

These results matter because they indicate that climate change is not only seen as an environmental issue by many young respondents, but also as a threat to personal futures, family security, and life planning. — derived by interpreting the meaning of high agreement across the six provided statements.

In the all-countries aggregate, three out of four or more respondents say the future is frightening (75%) and that people have failed to take care of the planet (83%), indicating broad climate-related distress and disillusionment among surveyed youth. — derived by reading and summarizing the All countries percentages.

The especially high values in the Philippines, India, and Brazil may signal that climate anxiety is particularly intense in some settings represented in this survey. — derived by comparing higher percentages across multiple columns for those countries.

Among the named countries, the Philippines records the highest percentage for four statements: family security is threatened (77%), less opportunity than their parents (70%), future is frightening (92%), and people have failed to take care of the planet (93%). — derived by identifying column maxima across country rows.
India has the highest value for "Humanity is doomed" at 74%. — derived by identifying the maximum in that column.
Brazil has the highest value for "Hesitant to have children" at 48%. — derived by identifying the maximum in that column.

Finland has the lowest percentage on four statements: humanity is doomed (43%), family security is threatened (30%), future is frightening (56%), and people have failed to take care of the planet (75%). — derived by identifying column minima across country rows.

Nigeria has the lowest value for hesitation to have children at 23%, and Finland has the lowest value for less opportunity than their parents at 42%. — derived by identifying minima in those two columns.

The spread between highest and lowest countries is largest for family security is threatened, at 47 percentage points from 30% in Finland to 77% in the Philippines. — derived by computing max-min for that statement.
speculative_claims: Cross-country differences may reflect differences in climate vulnerability, political discourse, media coverage, and economic conditions, but those causes are not identified in the provided metadata. — source: climate sociology and public opinion research.
Such views can shape youth engagement with politics, education, work, and family decisions. — source: youth studies and political behavior.

If similar attitudes persist, policymakers, educators, and mental-health practitioners may face greater pressure to address climate risk, trust in institutions, and youth wellbeing together rather than separately. — source: public policy and mental health.
